title: Count Squares from a Point
statement:
Build a collection of points on a grid that supports two operations:

  • SquareCounter() creates an empty collection.
  • add(point) stores the point [x, y]. The same point may be added many times; each copy is a separate point.
  • count(point) takes a query point [x, y] (which need not be stored) and returns how many ways you can pick three stored points that, together with the query point, form the corners of a square whose sides are parallel to the axes and whose area is greater than zero.

Choices that use different copies of a duplicated point count as different ways. Tests are a list of operations and their arguments; the first creates the collection, and the expected output has one entry per operation (null where nothing is returned).

examples.why: (4, 4) completes the square with side 3. After a second copy of (1, 4) is added there are two ways to pick the three other corners, so the count doubles to 2.

examples.out: [null, null, null, null, null, null, null, null, 3]
examples.why: Three squares of side 2 share the corner (2, 2): up-right, down-left and up-left. Looking only to the right of the query point finds just 1.
Copies of the query point itself would make a square of area 0, which does not count. (8, 8) has a diagonal partner at (5, 5) but is missing the corner (8, 5).

constraints: At most 3000 calls in total to add and count
hints: Fix the query point. A square with one corner there is decided by one more corner. Which one?
The opposite (diagonal) corner (px, py) decides the whole square: the other two corners are (x, py) and (px, y). It must satisfy |px − x| = |py − y| > 0.
Keep a count for each distinct point. For each stored point that can be the diagonal corner, add count(diagonal) · count(x, py) · count(px, y). Duplicates are then handled by the multiplication.

explain.intuition:
Call the query point (x, y). An axis-aligned square through it is fixed by its opposite corner (px, py): the side length is |px − x|, it must equal |py − y|, and the remaining two corners are forced to be (x, py) and (px, y). So instead of searching triples of points, loop over candidate diagonal corners and look the other two up.

Duplicates fit naturally with a count per point in a hash map: if the diagonal is stored 2 times and the other corners 3 and 1 times, there are 2 · 3 · 1 ways to pick one copy of each. To loop over fewer candidates, keep the points grouped by x. Every valid square has a corner (x, py) in the query's own column, so walk that column's points, compute the side d = py − y, and try both squares, the one to the right (px = x + d) and the one to the left (px = x − d). It is like indexing DOM nodes by one key so a lookup only touches one bucket.
steps: Keep cnt, a map from point to how many times it was added, and byX, a map from x to a map of y → count.
count([x, y]): for each (py, c) in byX[x] with py ≠ y, let d = py − y.
For both px = x + d and px = x − d, add c · cnt[(px, py)] · cnt[(px, y)] to the total.
pitfalls: Counting distinct points only. Every stored copy is a separate choice, so counts must be multiplied, not checked for presence.
Forgetting py ≠ y. A side of 0 adds zero-area "squares" built from copies of the query point.
Only checking squares on one side of the column, for example x + d. A square can lie left or right of the query point, as in the second example.

complexity.time: O(1) per add, O(k) per count where k is the number of distinct points in the query's column

solutions.title: Try every stored point as the diagonal, scan for the rest
solutions.idea: Keep a list of every added point. For each one that could be the opposite corner, count the matching other two corners by scanning the list again.

solutions.title: Point counts, scan distinct diagonals
solutions.idea: Store a count per distinct point. For a query, walk the distinct points, keep those on a diagonal, and multiply the three corner counts.

solutions.title: Index by column, try both sides
solutions.idea: Group counts by x. Every square through the query has a corner in the query's column, so only that column needs scanning; each point there gives one square to the right and one to the left.
solutions.time: O(1) add, O(points in the column) count

followups: Also count squares rotated at any angle. What decides such a square, and how many candidates does a query then have?
Points can also be removed. What changes in each data structure?
Count axis-aligned rectangles instead of squares. Why does that get more expensive?
